anatomy.lede: A body no bigger than a large dinner plate hangs from legs that reach across a room. Most of a Japanese spider crab is limb.

hotspots.label: Carapace
hotspots.text: The pear-shaped shell is covered in small, spike-like bumps. Young crabs have long spines for their size; on adults they are short and curve outwards.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Its eyestalks and antennae are reduced, and its senses seem less developed than those of many related crabs.

hotspots.label: Claw
hotspots.text: The claws sit on the first pair of legs. Females' are much shorter than males', and even shorter than the next pair of legs.

hotspots.label: Walking legs
hotspots.text: The legs keep growing after the crab reaches maturity, which is why old crabs reach such extraordinary spans.

hotspots.label: Leg tip
hotspots.text: It cannot swim. It walks slowly over the seafloor on its pointed leg tips, searching for food.

mind.lede: Little is known about how this giant lives day to day. Aquariums and divers describe a calm, solitary crab.

studies.title: Calm loners
studies.text: Japanese spider crabs spend much of their time slowly searching the seafloor for food. Even when kept together, they interact very little.

studies.title: Disguise is for the young
studies.text: Juveniles often camouflage themselves with sponges and other debris. Adults rarely bother, perhaps because their size already deters most predators.

survival.lede: For a young spider crab, safety means looking like the seabed; for an adult, being too big to bother with.

tactics.title: Living camouflage
tactics.text: Young crabs cover their shells with sponges and debris to blend in with the bottom.

tactics.title: Size and claws
tactics.text: Large adults are avoided by most predators and can fend off smaller attackers with their claws.

threats.title: Fishing
threats.text: It is caught as a delicacy in Japan, and catches have declined over the past 40 years. Data are too few to assess its conservation status.

threats.title: Protecting the breeding season
threats.text: Japanese law bans catching the crabs from January to April, their mating season, and restocking with farmed juveniles has been proposed.

life.lede: The world's longest-legged crab starts life as a speck of plankton, passing through four larval forms before it settles to the seabed.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Mating takes place in early spring, and the female carries her fertilised eggs on her body until they hatch.

stages.name: Prezoea
stages.text: The newly hatched larva is a prezoea, a stage that lasts only minutes before it moults.

stages.name: Zoea
stages.text: Two zoeal stages follow, swimming with the plankton near the surface.

stages.name: Megalopa
stages.text: The last larval stage, the megalopa, has the longest gap between moults. The planktonic stages together can last one to three months; 15–18 °C suits them best.

stages.name: Juvenile
stages.text: Young crabs settle on the seafloor, where they hide under sponges and other debris as they grow.

lifespan.value: Unverified; often said to exceed 50 years
